cards.body: Mindfulness isn't clearing your mind — that's impossible. It's noticing where your attention is, and choosing where it goes. Every time you catch your mind wandering and bring it back, that's one rep.
cards.title: Mindfulness is attention training, not mind-emptying

cards.body: You need something boring to return to, and your breath is perfect: always there, always rhythmic. Feel the air at your nostrils or the rise of your belly. When you drift, come back. That's the whole practice.
cards.title: The breath is your anchor

cards.body: Your first 2-minute sit: set a timer for 2 minutes. Sit upright, feet flat, hands in lap. Breathe normally and count exhales — one, two, three… up to ten, then start over. Lost count? Begin at one again. That's not failure, that's the rep.
Start embarrassingly small. Two minutes daily beats thirty minutes once a month. Tiny sessions build the habit; the habit builds the calm. Scale up only when two minutes feels too easy.

choices: Thinking about nothing for the full session
Noticing your mind wandered and returning to the breath
cards.explain: The rep IS the return. A wandering mind isn't a failed session — noticing the wander and coming back is literally the exercise.
cards.q: What counts as a successful meditation rep?

questions.explain: It's about directing attention, not achieving blankness. The wandering-and-returning is the workout.

choices: It makes you fall asleep faster
It's always there and naturally rhythmic
questions.explain: The anchor just needs to be boring and available — the breath is both, everywhere you go.
questions.q: Why is the breath a good anchor?

choices: Start over at one — that's the rep
Guess where you were and continue
questions.explain: Losing count IS the practice moment. Restarting at one is the rep, not a failure.
questions.q: You lose count at 'seven' during breath counting. Best move?

questions.explain: Frequency builds the habit; marathon sessions build dread. Two minutes daily, then scale up.
questions.q: For a beginner, the smartest session length is…

questions.explain: Each return is one rep. Twenty returns means twenty reps of attention training.
questions.q: Your mind wanders 20 times in 2 minutes. That session was…

flashcards.back: Noticing where your attention is and choosing where it goes — attention training, not mind-emptying.
A neutral, always-available focus point (nostrils or belly) you return to when your mind drifts.
Catching your mind wandering and gently bringing it back to the anchor. That's the whole practice.
Two minutes daily beats a long session once a month — tiny reps build the habit.

cards.body: A thought appears like a cloud — you don't have to chase it or fight it. Fighting thoughts gives them energy; noticing them lets them pass. You're the sky, not the weather.
cards.title: Thoughts are weather, not commands

cards.body: When a thought hooks you, silently label it: 'planning,' 'worrying,' 'remembering.' Labeling creates a tiny gap between you and the thought — and the gap is where calm lives.
cards.title: The labeling technique

cards.body: The itch experiment: next sit, an itch will arrive right on schedule. Don't scratch immediately — observe it for 30 seconds like a scientist. Watch it peak, fade, and return. That observation muscle is mindfulness in action.

Trade the inner critic for a coach. When you catch yourself thinking 'I'm terrible at this,' relabel it: 'I'm training.' Self-compassion isn't softness — it's what keeps you coming back tomorrow. Criticism quits; kindness repeats.

choices: Argue with it until it loses
Label it 'worrying' and return to the breath
Force yourself to think of nothing
cards.explain: Labeling defuses the loop without a fight. Arguing feeds it; the label-and-return starves it.
cards.q: A stressful thought keeps looping. The mindful response?

choices: You observe thoughts without chasing them
questions.explain: Clouds pass whether you chase them or not. Observation, not control, is the skill.

choices: Creates distance between you and the thought
questions.explain: The label creates a gap — you're watching the thought instead of being inside it.
questions.q: Labeling a thought as 'planning' does what?

questions.explain: Watching the itch peak and fade without reacting builds the same muscle you use on thoughts.

choices: 'I'll try harder to empty my mind'
questions.explain: Self-compassion keeps you returning; the critic makes you quit. Training beats judging.
questions.q: Your inner critic says you're bad at meditating. Best reframe?

questions.explain: Resistance feeds the loop. Noticing and labeling lets it pass on its own.

flashcards.back: Thoughts pass like clouds — you observe them instead of chasing or fighting them.
Silently naming a thought ('planning,' 'worrying') to create distance from it.
Observe an itch for 30 seconds without scratching — training observation over reaction.
Treating yourself like a trainee, not a failure — it's what keeps the habit alive.

cards.body: Habits attach to cues. Meditate right after something you already do daily — morning coffee, lunch, brushing teeth. Same trigger, same cushion, and the habit builds itself.
cards.title: Same time, same place

cards.body: Guided sessions teach you the moves; silent sits build the muscle. Start guided for two weeks, then mix in silent minutes. Neither is better — they're the training wheels and the bike.
cards.title: Guided vs. silent

cards.body: The 8-week expectation reset: studies on mindfulness programs typically run about 8 weeks before measuring benefits. Expecting transformation in 3 days is like expecting muscle after 3 pushups. Commit to the reps, not the rush.
Miss a day? Never miss twice. One skipped day is life; two is a new habit of quitting. Come back tomorrow, no guilt, no 'starting over.'

choices: Only meditate when you feel stressed
Wait until you have 30 free minutes
Attach it to an existing daily habit
cards.explain: Habit stacking — same cue, same place — beats motivation every time. Motivation fades; cues persist.
cards.q: The best way to make meditation stick?

choices: Meditating on a tall stack of cushions
Linking meditation to something you already do daily
questions.explain: The existing routine becomes the trigger — no willpower required to remember.

choices: Learning the moves as a beginner
questions.explain: Guided sessions teach the technique; once you know the moves, silent sits build the muscle.
questions.q: Guided meditation is most useful for…

questions.explain: Research programs typically measure benefits around 8 weeks. Reps, not rush.

choices: Start the streak over from zero
questions.explain: Never miss twice. Guilt and punishment kill habits; a calm return keeps them.
questions.q: You skipped yesterday's session. Best move?

choices: Habits attach to cues, not motivation
questions.explain: A consistent cue fires the habit automatically. Motivation is unreliable; cues are not.
questions.q: Why does 'same time, same place' work?

flashcards.back: Attaching meditation to an existing daily routine so the cue triggers the habit.
Guided teaches the moves; silent builds the muscle. Use both.
Mindfulness benefits are typically measured after ~8 weeks — commit to reps, not rush.
One skip is life, two is quitting. Come back the next day, guilt-free.
